analysis.one_liner: Lets people injured by glyphosate exposure sue manufacturers and blocks federal funds for an immunity-granting defense order.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced February 20, 2026 with bipartisan sponsorship, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responds to an executive order issued February 18, 2026 that invoked the Defense Production Act to boost domestic supply of elemental phosphorus and glyphosate herbicides. It bars any federal money from carrying out that order, and it creates a federal right to sue any manufacturer, distributor, or seller of these chemicals for injuries they cause. It also wipes out any immunity or 'federal contractor' defense a company might claim under the order, and lets courts award compensatory and punitive damages plus attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits: People who say they were sickened by exposure to glyphosate herbicides or elemental phosphorus — farmworkers, herbicide applicators, and communities near spraying — plus the estates and families of people who died. They get a new federal court right to sue manufacturers for medical costs, lost income, and punitive damages, with attorney's fees covered, even for exposures that happened before the bill passes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to glyphosate and their families

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal cause of action letting anyone injured by exposure to elemental phosphorus or a glyphosate-based herbicide sue the manufacturer, distributor, or seller in federal district court, with no minimum dollar threshold.
Allows compensatory damages (medical expenses, lost income, pain and suffering, wrongful death), punitive damages, injunctions, and attorney's fees and costs.

Waives and nullifies any immunity the companies might claim under section 707 of the Defense Production Act, and bars them from defending lawsuits by saying the product was made in compliance with the executive order or any federal authorization.
Prohibits any federal funds from being used to implement, administer, or enforce the February 18, 2026 executive order on phosphorus and glyphosate supplies.
Preserves all existing state-law claims and pending lawsuits, applies to claims arising before, on, or after enactment, and does not preempt state law.

analysis.who_pays: Glyphosate and phosphorus manufacturers — companies like Bayer's Monsanto unit, the main Roundup maker — would face injury lawsuits, punitive damages, and fee awards. Indirectly, farmers and defense programs could bear costs if litigation pressure raises prices or disrupts supply of these chemicals.

drawbacks.text: The executive order it defunds was issued to ensure an adequate defense supply of elemental phosphorus — a chemical used in munitions — and glyphosate; blocking its implementation could complicate that supply chain.

The bill applies retroactively to claims arising before enactment and creates a sweeping new federal tort right, which companies would argue invites a wave of litigation and could lead makers to limit or exit the glyphosate market, raising costs for the farmers who depend on the herbicide.

It covers a broad universe of 'covered entities' — anyone who manufactures, distributes, formulates, supplies, or sells these chemicals — not just the original manufacturers, spreading legal exposure across the supply chain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who believe glyphosate exposure caused their illness, the bill is a direct remedy: it removes the legal shields the executive order would provide and opens federal court with fee support, which matters because these cases are expensive. The honest costs are on the other side of the ledger: possible defense-supply disruption and litigation pressure on a herbicide most of American agriculture uses. The bill does not ban glyphosate or restrict use, so it leaves availability intact while shifting the risk of harm onto the companies that profit from the product.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on February 20, 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action on it; it is still alive while this Congress is in session.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Massie introduced the bill on February 20, 2026 with original cosponsors from both parties: Chellie Pingree (D), Lauren Boebert (R), Nancy Mace (R), and Ro Khanna (D).
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and no other action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the record since.
Sixteen members have signed on as cosponsors: 12 Democrats and 4 Republicans.

The bill targets an executive order issued two days earlier, on February 18, 2026, titled 'Promoting the National Defense by Ensuring an Adequate Supply of Elemental Phosphorus and Glyphosate-Based Herbicides,' and specifically nullifies manufacturer immunity under the Defense Production Act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, glyphosate manufacturers. The bill exists precisely to strip the immunity and protections the February 2026 executive order provides, and with no committee or floor action, those protections remain in place and injured people still lack the new federal right to sue the bill would create.

sides.party_line_note: Support crosses party lines — the sponsor is a Republican joined by 12 Democratic and 4 Republican cosponsors — but with no committee or floor votes, the record shows nothing about how opposition would split.

industries.note: The bill strips these companies of any immunity the February 2026 defense order provides and lets injured people sue them for compensatory and punitive damages plus fees. Their interest is in keeping those protections, which is the opposite of what people exposed to the chemical want.

industries.industry: Defense supply chain for elemental phosphorus
industries.note: By defunding the executive order meant to ensure an adequate defense supply of elemental phosphorus, the bill could complicate procurement of a chemical used in munitions, even as it opens liability for harms the chemical causes.

Farmers are not covered entities under the bill, so they face no new liability for spraying glyphosate; but if litigation pressure pushes manufacturers to limit supply or raise prices, agriculture could pay more for a herbicide it depends on.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term bill with no committee action since February has little path forward: House Judiciary rarely holds hearings or markups on bills without leadership backing, and without it this bill is likely to sit unacted on until this Congress ends on January 3, 2027. The realistic chance of becoming law is low unless it is attached to a larger, must-pass bill.
